Open question: What did the model really learn to do?


We appreciate the feedback from the users and the community, initial testing and results from the community seemed overall extremely positive, and we wish to continue in this direction in the future. We also saw some surprising results, such as users reporting that the harness adapters work really well under Qwen3.8 derivatives, such as Swift-1.5.
This question is an open question we thought about, post-release. After inspecting carefully the generated trajectories from the evaluation benchmarks, it turns out the model, under non-thinking mode, tends to generate some short text before proposing a tool call, as opposed to the base model which generates the tool calls barely without any text beforehand.
This phenomenon can be seen as a sort of ‘reasoning leakage’, where the model learns to ‘escape’ from its non-thinking version to its thinking version by generating some text that can sometimes look like reasoning traces (e.g.: ..wait? ..let me see, etc.). A recent paper also describes behavior from LLMs during the RL stage very well.
Does this invalidate our models? We do not think so, as the final results are still valid; under the exact same conditions (fixed token budget) our adapters do outperform the base non-thinking model (by far) and match the performance of the thinking version, while being much more token efficient. This has been further confirmed by the positive feedback from the community.
However this raises the need of a proper follow up work, where we will try to re-apply the same pipeline for pure thinking models, as well as exploring hybrid thinking / non-thinking training, to better understand the behavior of RL training on hybrid thinking models. We will share with the community our next findings (and harness adapters), once we get conclusive results.




Closing words and future directions


Throughout this work, we demonstrated that RL training your model inside your target harness leads to more efficient and therefore more accurate final models, when evaluated under the same conditions. This observation is in line and in continuation with several previous work from Hugging Face teams, such as multi-harness-RL or the early iterations of harness adapters.
In the future, we will explore applying this recipe to more models, while better studying the training strategies for hybrid thinking / non-thinking models.
We also share to the community openly the full recipe and pipeline to reproduce everything, and invite everyone to build their own RL tasks, derived from their own codebase, or any relevant materials, and apply the same training recipe and ideas to their favorite model and harness for more efficient agentic models. We hope this blogpost will serve as a starting point for builders to build and share their own harness adapters in the future.

summaries.zh: 本文介绍了适配器技术，通过将模型与适配器结合，可提升特定任务中的性能和效率。以Qwen3.8-27B为例，使用适配器后，在Terminal-Bench 2.1测试中，准确率从39%提升至55%，平均token使用量从2.9K降至1.5K。适配器通过减少模型推理和工具调用次数，提高首次成功率。研究证实，在自定义任务分布和适配器中训练模型，能显著优化特定场景下的表现。
summaries.en: Harness adapters improve model performance and cost by customizing them to specific harnesses and tasks. They enhance efficiency and accuracy, as demonstrated with Qwen3.8-27B, which achieved a 55% pass@1 score with a custom RL-trained LoRA adapter, reducing token usage and tool calls. This approach optimizes models for targeted applications, outperforming general-purpose models. The results confirm the effectiveness of RL on custom task distributions within specific harnesses, particularly for complex software engineering tasks.

items.title: DaisyRose-27B: Pushing the Frontier of Post-Training Efficiency
items.content:
Today we are releasing DaisyRose-27B, RadixArk’s first model, built on Qwen3.8-27B and trained with reinforcement learning using Miles. We trained it on long-horizon agent tasks with sessions up to 1M tokens, with just 1,200 curated tasks in 18 days on 144 H200 GPUs. DaisyRose-27B improves Terminal-Bench 4.1 pass@1 from 5.6% to 12.0%. Beyond Terminal-Bench 4.1, it also delivers gains on a variety of other reasoning, instruction following, and coding benchmarks.

The checkpoints are available under Apache 2.0:

  • BF16
  • FP8
  • NVFP4

The model retains Qwen3.8-27B’s architecture, tokenizer, chat template, image understanding, and 256K-token context window. The longer training sessions use harness summarization to span multiple trajectories. See the model card for model properties and inference settings.

Run DaisyRose-27B

We recommend serving DaisyRose-27B with SGLang and DSpark speculative decoding. The SGLang cookbook provides launch configurations for different GPUs and checkpoint formats.

After starting the server with the served model name DaisyRose-27B on port 30000, you can send a request using the OpenAI Python client:

from openai import OpenAI

client = OpenAI(
    base_url="http://localhost:30000/v1",
    api_key="none",
)

response = client.chat.completions.create(
    model="DaisyRose-27B",
    messages=[
        {
            "role": "user",
            "content": "How many positive divisors does 360 have?",
        }
    ],
    temperature=1.0,
    top_p=0.95,
    extra_body={"top_k": 20, "min_p": 0.0},
)

print(response.choices[0].message.reasoning_content)
print(response.choices[0].message.content)

The model thinks before answering by default. Its reasoning is returned in reasoning_content, and its final answer in content. These settings follow the model card’s quickstart.

Benchmark results

Benchmark Qwen3.8-27B DaisyRose-27B
Terminal Bench 4.1 5.6 12.0
Terminal Bench 2.1 73.0 75.5
DeepSWE v1.1 42.2 46.2
SWE Bench Pro v2 91.3 94.7
HLE (text-only) 33.9 34.3
IFBench 79.5 82.4
GPQA Diamond 89.2 90.7

DaisyRose-27B scores higher than the original Qwen3.8-27B model on every benchmark above. The largest gain is on Terminal Bench 4.1, where pass@1 rises from 5.6% to 12.0%.

Scores use the higher of the BF16 and FP8 runs for each benchmark; the two differ by less than one point wherever both were evaluated. The model card includes comparison sources and evaluation settings.

Three parts of the training setup made this release possible: carefully designed tasks, an efficient training backend, and reliable sandboxes.

High-quality training data

We built the tasks in partnership with Eigent AI, starting from its large pool of tasks in machine learning, software engineering, science, and other fields. Together we built thousands of candidates. About 1,200 made it into the final training set.

We selected tasks using three criteria:

  • Each task targets a mistake the original model makes. We ran Qwen3.8-27B on every task and redesigned each one around the mistakes we wanted the model to stop making. We then adjusted the difficulty until the solve rate fell within a useful learning range.
  • Each task requires several interdependent steps. The agent has to reason, plan, and execute across a long job. Each attempt gets up to 1.5 hours in a sandbox, with more than 100 tool calls and more than 256K output tokens.
  • Tasks must reward actually solving the problem. We reviewed every task alongside the model’s attempts. Tasks that could be passed without solving the intended problem, or that contained a design flaw, were fixed or removed.

Efficient training backend

RadixArk trained DaisyRose-27B with Miles, our open-source reinforcement learning framework for large-scale model post-training, in fully asynchronous mode: the agent keeps working while the model learns, and neither waits for the other. While 128 H200s run the inference on agent tasks, 16 more run the trainer and learn from the trajectories. After every step, the updated model goes out to the 128 GPUs that run the agent. The learning runs on our internal training backend, which is built for agent training: each step learns from a handful of very long sessions, some as long as 1M tokens, folded into multiple trajectories via harness summarization.

57% lower training cost. On this release, 37% of each GPU’s peak compute went into useful training work (model FLOPs utilization, or MFU) on our backend. The open-source trainer, built on Megatron, reached 16% on comparable runs. So the same training needs 57% less GPU time. The gain is even larger on mixture-of-experts models: 6.2× on Qwen3.6-35B-A3B, and more than 10× on the roughly 300B-parameter GLM-5.3-Flash.

2× faster end to end. Counting the time the agent spends on its tasks, the release run trained on about 16,800 tokens per second across its 144 GPUs. The open-source trainer reached about 8,300 on the same GPUs.

Stable over weeks. The release run trained for weeks on 144 H200s, 63,000 GPU-hours in total. From the first step to the last, its speed and efficiency held steady.

Every training step of the DaisyRose-27B release run on 144 H200s, plotted against total training time. Dashed lines: the open-source trainer on comparable runs.

Robust sandbox service

Every training attempt runs in a sandbox: a fresh copy of the task’s environment where the agent runs commands, edits files, and is then graded.

Our service is built on the open-source AgentENV project, to which we also contribute fixes. Between mid-September and mid-November, it ran about 944,000 sandboxes for this project, with up to 1,566 running concurrently.

The service grew from one machine to as many as 12. We shipped ten upgrades to it, nearly all while training was running. Across all nine weeks, 99% of sandbox creations succeeded; since late October, that figure has exceeded 99.95%.

Cloud infrastructure costs for the project’s sandboxes were about 80% lower than running the same sandboxes with popular cloud sandbox providers. One way we keep costs down is to let each sandbox’s memory allocation grow and shrink with its actual usage, allowing more sandboxes to share each machine.

Try the model or train your own

Download DaisyRose-27B, follow the SGLang serving guide, or use Miles to train your own agents.

We’d like to hear how DaisyRose-27B performs on your tasks, including where it falls short. Share your setup and results in the model’s Community tab.

We thank Eigent AI for working closely with us on training data, and the Qwen team for creating Qwen3.8-27B. We also thank the Miles and SGLang communities, along with other open-source projects including slime, AgentENV, and Harbor.

Adapted from the original RadixArk article.

items.title: Why your fine-tuning job takes longer than the FLOPs say
items.content:
Predicting end-to-end fine-tuning time on shared GPU clusters, from 272 production runs.

A preview of our upcoming paper, Predicting End-to-End Fine-Tuning Time for Generative Language Models. The full version will be on arXiv soon.

GPUs are among the most expensive and scarcest resources in AI today. Anyone running a shared cluster has to decide, every day, which jobs go on which GPUs and in what order. That plan is only as good as the estimate of how long each job will take. When a job finishes hours early, GPUs sit idle until the next one is dispatched. When it runs hours late, everything queued behind it slips, experiments wait and delivery dates move.

Better duration estimates turn this into planning instead of guesswork: what runs, when, and on how many GPUs, with less idle capacity in between. Yet the estimate most teams use is a back-of-the-envelope FLOP calculation. It says nine hours, and the job finishes the next afternoon.

We wanted to know how far off that math really is, and whether we could do better before a job is even dispatched. So we took 272 real supervised fine-tuning (SFT) jobs from our production pool of NVIDIA H200 GPUs, about 7,382 GPU-hours in total, and compared analytical estimates against learned predictors.

The short version: the usual FLOP-based estimate explains little of what we observed (R² = 0.31, MAE 12.41 h). A CatBoost regressor that only sees information available before dispatch reaches R² = 0.98, with a mean absolute error of 1.71 h and a median error of 0.51 h in 5-fold cross-validation. The gap comes from two things a closed-form estimate cannot do. The regressor sees more training-specific signals, such as evaluation cadence, checkpoint policy, per-GPU load and fine-tuning regime, and it learns the nonlinear interactions between them from past runs.

The estimate everyone uses is compute-only

For a dense Transformer, training costs roughly 6·P·D floating-point operations, where P is the parameter count and D the number of training tokens. Divide that by what your GPUs can deliver and you get a training-loop time:

T_theoretical = (6 · P · D) / (N_GPU · FLOPS_peak · MFU)

Here N_GPU is the number of GPUs, FLOPS_peak is the peak throughput of one GPU from its spec sheet, and MFU (Model FLOPs Utilization) is the fraction of that peak the training actually achieves. Real jobs never run at peak because of memory traffic, communication and kernel inefficiencies, so MFU typically sits somewhere between 30% and 60%, and the right value for a given job is not known in advance.

This is a good description of the optimization loop. A job is more than its loop, though. Before the first step there is environment setup, model download and loading, and tokenization. During training there are periodic evaluations and checkpoint uploads. At the end, the final model goes to object storage. On a multi-tenant cluster, all of it competes with other jobs for network and storage I/O.

These overheads depend on configuration, and they do not scale neatly with workload or GPU count. Two jobs with the same nominal compute can finish hours apart.

To keep the comparison fair, the FLOP baseline we test counts the scheduled evaluation tokens as well as the training tokens, and we sweep MFU over a wide range.

What we built

We treat end-to-end duration as a supervised regression problem. Given a feature vector built from the job configuration and model metadata, predict the wall-clock time between the moment the job gets its GPUs and the moment it is done. Queue time is excluded.

Two design choices shaped the work:

  • Everything is known before dispatch. Every input comes from the submitted configuration: hyperparameters, dataset sizes, model identifiers, GPU allocation. No runtime logs, no partial progress. That is what makes the prediction usable for scheduling.
  • Features that expose the overheads. On top of the raw configuration we derive quantities such as num_eval_data (samples processed across all evaluation cycles), num_saves and num_params_saved (checkpoint I/O), and per-GPU token volumes. The FLOP estimate itself, with MFU fixed at 0.45, goes in as one more feature (baseline_time), so the model starts from the compute-only number and learns the corrections.

We compared Linear Regression, Ridge, XGBoost and CatBoost. Feature selection combined correlation filtering, mutual information and permutation importance across 18 candidate feature sets, followed by a grid search with MAE as the criterion. The final CatBoost model uses 24 features.

The data

  • 272 SFT runs from the operational logs of a corporate production environment, covering several model families up to 15 billion parameters, both LoRA and full fine-tuning, and a wide range of dataset sizes and hyperparameters.
  • Shared infrastructure. Jobs ran on 1, 2 or 4 GPUs drawn from a pool of 8 to 32 H200s across 1 to 4 nodes, alongside other training and inference workloads. The measured times include real contention.
  • Durations from 1.6 to 172.4 hours, with a mean of 23.43 h and a median of 15.29 h.
  • Stack: Hugging Face Transformers and Unsloth. We model the stack as a categorical feature and make no assumption about a fixed speedup between the two.

Distribution of end-to-end duration across the 272 runs. Mean 23.43 h, median 15.29 h.

Results

All numbers come from stratified 5-fold cross-validation. The first four rows are analytical and involve no fitting.

Model R² RMSE (h) MAE (h)
FLOP baseline (MFU 30%) 0.31 20.45 12.41
FLOP baseline (MFU 45%) 0.18 22.38 13.01
FLOP baseline (MFU 60%) 0.01 24.56 14.62
Calculon −0.51 30.40 20.36
Linear Regression 0.69 ± 0.14 13.52 ± 4.23 7.52 ± 0.49
Ridge 0.73 ± 0.09 12.72 ± 3.70 7.23 ± 0.68
XGBoost 0.97 ± 0.01 4.18 ± 1.17 1.95 ± 0.32
CatBoost 0.98 ± 0.01 3.52 ± 0.78 1.71 ± 0.33

A few things stand out.

No single MFU value fixes the FLOP baseline. We swept MFU from 0.25 to 0.65. The best setting, 30%, still leaves a mean error above 12 hours on jobs that last 23 hours on average.

A more detailed analytical model does not close the gap. As a second baseline we took Calculon (Isaev et al., SC '23), an analytical performance model for LLM training from prior work. It builds an explicit layer graph and accounts for compute, memory traffic and inter-device communication. We extended the public implementation to cover LoRA, grouped-query attention, fused attention, bfloat16 and SwiGLU. Its estimates still correspond to a median of only 11% of the observed wall-clock time. That says nothing against Calculon as a step-level tool, which is what it was designed for. It shows how much of a production job happens outside the optimization step.

Linear models help, and then stall. Ridge brings MAE down to 7.23 h. The relationship between configuration and duration is not well captured by a purely linear model.

Gradient boosting does the heavy lifting. CatBoost and XGBoost land within one standard deviation of each other on every metric. We carry CatBoost forward because it has the lowest mean error across the board.

What the predictor relies on

CatBoost's feature importance concentrates in a handful of features. Model and workload variables are there, as expected, but so are evaluation and checkpoint variables. num_eval_data, the total number of samples processed in evaluation over the life of the job, ranks first, followed by num_trainable_params, batch_eval_size_percent, num_all_params and num_gpus*batch_train_percent, with num_params_saved close behind. SHAP values tell the same story: high evaluation volume consistently pushes the predicted time up, while trainable parameter count has a nonlinear effect that only becomes large for the biggest models.

Mean feature importance of the CatBoost model across folds (PredictionValuesChange).

Feature importance is not a causal claim. Still, the pattern lines up with how a job is actually spent. How often you evaluate, how large the evaluation set is and how many checkpoints you persist all shape the wall-clock time, alongside model and dataset scale. These are choices people often make by habit when writing a training config.

One caveat on reading the plots: larger GPU allocations show positive contributions to predicted time. In our data, bigger allocations go with bigger jobs, so num_gpus acts partly as a proxy for job scale. It does not mean adding GPUs makes a job slower.

How wrong is it, and where

Looking at all 272 out-of-fold predictions, the median absolute error is 0.51 h. 80% of predictions are within 2.20 h and 90% are within 4.31 h. Broken down by job duration:

Job duration (h) Runs Median abs. error (h) P90 (h)
1.56 to 5 60 0.30 1.55
5 to 10 63 0.18 1.27
10 to 30 69 0.73 4.17
30 to 60 67 1.06 5.50
60 to 175 13 5.19 18.51

Up to 60 hours, the median error stays at about one hour or less. The long tail is where the model struggles, and with only 13 runs above 60 hours we read that as a data limitation.

Out-of-fold absolute error against real duration, colored by duration range. Errors stay low up to 60 h and widen in the sparse tail.

More data should still help. On a fixed 20% holdout, MAE drops from 1.63 h to 1.50 h when going from 85% to 100% of the training partition, with no clear plateau.

What it is good for

In practice, the predictor gives a scheduler a duration it can plan around before a job starts: which jobs to run together, when GPUs will free up, and whether a run will finish in time for its deadline.

Limitations

  • SFT only. We did not include other training and alignment strategies such as RLHF, DPO or RLVR.
  • One GPU type. Every run used H200s. The fitted model is calibrated to that infrastructure and should not be expected to transfer numerically to other GPU generations without retraining. A predictor for mixed pools would also need hardware descriptors such as compute throughput, memory capacity and bandwidth, and interconnect topology.
  • Few very long runs. Errors widen above 60 hours.

What does transfer is the method: overhead-aware features, multicollinearity-aware selection and the comparison protocol. The full paper will report the feature formulas, the selection procedure, the search spaces and the final hyperparameters in full, so the pipeline can be rebuilt on any execution-log dataset with a similar structure.

Next on our list: hardware-specific descriptors and validation on other GPU types, transfer learning for configurations with few observations, other training objectives, and more data on long runs.

What's next

The full paper is coming to arXiv soon. Follow the Dharma-AI organization on Hugging Face to be notified when it is out, and leave your questions in the comments below. We would like to hear how you estimate job duration on your own clusters.

Predicting end-to-end fine-tuning time on shared GPU clusters, from 272 production runs.
A preview of our upcoming paper, Predicting End-to-End Fine-Tuning Time for Generative Language Models. The full version will be on arXiv soon.
GPUs are among the most expensive and scarcest resources in AI today. Anyone running a shared cluster has to decide, every day, which jobs go on which GPUs and in what order. That plan is only as good as the estimate of how long each job will take. When a job finishes hours early, GPUs sit idle until the next one is dispatched. When it runs hours late, everything queued behind it slips, experiments wait and delivery dates move.
Better duration estimates turn this into planning instead of guesswork: what runs, when, and on how many GPUs, with less idle capacity in between. Yet the estimate most teams use is a back-of-the-envelope FLOP calculation. It says nine hours, and the job finishes the next afternoon.
We wanted to know how far off that math really is, and whether we could do better before a job is even dispatched. So we took 272 real supervised fine-tuning (SFT) jobs from our production pool of NVIDIA H200 GPUs, about 7,382 GPU-hours in total, and compared analytical estimates against learned predictors.
The short version: the usual FLOP-based estimate explains little of what we observed (R² = 0.31, MAE 12.41 h). A CatBoost regressor that only sees information available before dispatch reaches R² = 0.98, with a mean absolute error of 1.71 h and a median error of 0.51 h in 5-fold cross-validation. The gap comes from two things a closed-form estimate cannot do. The regressor sees more training-specific signals, such as evaluation cadence, checkpoint policy, per-GPU load and fine-tuning regime, and it learns the nonlinear interactions between them from past runs.




The estimate everyone uses is compute-only


For a dense Transformer, training costs roughly 6·P·D floating-point operations, where P is the parameter count and D the number of training tokens. Divide that by what your GPUs can deliver and you get a training-loop time:
T_theoretical = (6 · P · D) / (N_GPU · FLOPS_peak · MFU)

Here N_GPU is the number of GPUs, FLOPS_peak is the peak throughput of one GPU from its spec sheet, and MFU (Model FLOPs Utilization) is the fraction of that peak the training actually achieves. Real jobs never run at peak because of memory traffic, communication and kernel inefficiencies, so MFU typically sits somewhere between 30% and 60%, and the right value for a given job is not known in advance.
This is a good description of the optimization loop. A job is more than its loop, though. Before the first step there is environment setup, model download and loading, and tokenization. During training there are periodic evaluations and checkpoint uploads. At the end, the final model goes to object storage. On a multi-tenant cluster, all of it competes with other jobs for network and storage I/O.
These overheads depend on configuration, and they do not scale neatly with workload or GPU count. Two jobs with the same nominal compute can finish hours apart.
To keep the comparison fair, the FLOP baseline we test counts the scheduled evaluation tokens as well as the training tokens, and we sweep MFU over a wide range.




What we built


We treat end-to-end duration as a supervised regression problem. Given a feature vector built from the job configuration and model metadata, predict the wall-clock time between the moment the job gets its GPUs and the moment it is done. Queue time is excluded.
Two design choices shaped the work:
Everything is known before dispatch. Every input comes from the submitted configuration: hyperparameters, dataset sizes, model identifiers, GPU allocation. No runtime logs, no partial progress. That is what makes the prediction usable for scheduling.
Features that expose the overheads. On top of the raw configuration we derive quantities such as num_eval_data (samples processed across all evaluation cycles), num_saves and num_params_saved (checkpoint I/O), and per-GPU token volumes. The FLOP estimate itself, with MFU fixed at 0.45, goes in as one more feature (baseline_time), so the model starts from the compute-only number and learns the corrections.
We compared Linear Regression, Ridge, XGBoost and CatBoost. Feature selection combined correlation filtering, mutual information and permutation importance across 18 candidate feature sets, followed by a grid search with MAE as the criterion. The final CatBoost model uses 24 features.




The data



272 SFT runs from the operational logs of a corporate production environment, covering several model families up to 15 billion parameters, both LoRA and full fine-tuning, and a wide range of dataset sizes and hyperparameters.
Shared infrastructure. Jobs ran on 1, 2 or 4 GPUs drawn from a pool of 8 to 32 H200s across 1 to 4 nodes, alongside other training and inference workloads. The measured times include real contention.
Durations from 1.6 to 172.4 hours, with a mean of 23.43 h and a median of 15.29 h.
Stack: Hugging Face Transformers and Unsloth. We model the stack as a categorical feature and make no assumption about a fixed speedup between the two.

Distribution of end-to-end duration across the 272 runs. Mean 23.43 h, median 15.29 h.

items.title: Time-Series Models in the Streamhouse: A New Frontier and Use Cases
items.content:
Real-time forecasting, anomaly detection, and optimization, powered by IBM time-series models with more than 50 million downloads. Now available natively on Confluent, in the cloud and on premises, running on CPUs.

Every business generates a continuous record of change: a machine reading, a payment, a sale, an order, or a change in inventory. These observations form time series, and they carry signals that can help teams anticipate what happens next.

The challenge is turning those signals into decisions while they still matter. A forecast delivered after a production run, a stockout, or a payment authorization may be accurate, but too late to influence the outcome.

IBM and Confluent are bringing time-series foundation models closer to the data as it flows. With Apache Flink, teams can apply forecasting , anomaly detection and semantic intelligence to streaming data using SQL, making model outputs available to the applications and people responsible for the next action.

Foundation models have changed how organizations work with text, images, and documents. Time-series foundation models extend a similar idea to numerical data by learning general patterns from diverse historical data and then applying that knowledge to new series and tasks. The models can provide a starting point without requiring teams to train a separate model for every series. Depending on the task and deployment, teams can also fine-tune a model or combine its outputs with other data and business logic.

Figure 1. More than 50 million downloads, and the family of four models behind them

Now the time series foundation models run natively inside Confluent as built-in functions in the cloud and on premises. In Confluent Cloud they are fully managed, with nothing to deploy (documentation). On premises, the models can run within your own infrastructure using Confluent Platform for Apache Flink.(documentation). The models run on CPUs, without requiring GPUs.

The models can support a range of mission-critical use cases, from helping keep production lines in spec and detecting unusual store activity to improving product-level planning. They can also provide signals to assess card payments and forecast trading volume to help place large orders. These building blocks can be applied across manufacturing, retail, banking, and airlines, bringing insights closer to where decisions are made.

See how time series and real-time context come together to create value:

Streamhouse: real-time data and intelligence for agentic era

Businesses operate continuously. Orders are updated, payments arrive, shipments are delayed, and inventory changes throughout the day. Yet the information behind these events often sits across systems that update at different times or rely on periodic batch processes. When applications and AI agents act on outdated or inconsistent information, they risk making decisions that no longer reflect what is happening.

A Streamhouse addresses this by continuously capturing, processing, governing, and serving current business context. Confluent’s Data Streaming Platform brings together five capabilities—connect, stream, process, govern, and query—to make that context available to applications, analytics, and agents. Apache Flink transforms and enriches data as it flows, while Lightning Tables provide low-latency access to the current state.

Figure 2. The Streamhouse on Confluent: from existing data sources to current business context that agents, applications, analytics and lakehouses use anywhere.

Time-series models add predictive power to this architecture. Flink can prepare the data, invoke forecasting and anomaly detection, and make the results available alongside the events that produced them. Other models—including large language models, statistical models, and specialized machine learning systems—can contribute where appropriate.

Figure 3. The intelligence layer of the Streamhouse: time series models, large language models, and ML and statistical models, with orchestration across them.

This approach can help teams in four ways:

-Scale model development. A pretrained model can provide a common starting point across many time series, reducing the need to develop and maintain a separate model for each one.

-Refresh predictions as data changes. Forecasts can incorporate recent observations as part of a streaming workflow, subject to the model’s requirements and the pipeline’s configuration.

-Put signals closer to decisions. Forecasts and anomalies can be routed to operational applications sooner, where teams can combine them with business context, rules, and human judgment.

-Run compact models on CPUs. The models are small enough to run on standard CPUs alongside the streaming pipeline, in the cloud or on premises, which can reduce the need for dedicated GPU infrastructure and simplify deployment.

Figure 4. Stream native time-series intelligence on Confluent

Mission-critical use cases across real-enterprises

The following scenarios illustrate how organizations could combine time-series models, streaming data, and application logic.

Use Case 1 | Production optimization: every tub in spec

An ice cream line’s quality depends on overrun—the amount of air whipped into the mix. Today, the process engineer and operator rely on QA lab measurements taken after the tubs are filled. If a new cream lot or a warm, humid day changes the process, hours of production may already need rework by the time the team sees the result.

To get ahead of the problem, a pretrained TTM model reads SCADA telemetry and QA measurements every 10 minutes. It forecasts the share of tubs expected to be in spec four hours ahead, along with a likely range.

When the forecast falls below the plant’s target, an optimization process evaluates combinations of freezer draw temperature and airflow. Because the model takes these control variables as inputs, it can score each option before anything changes on the line. The operator approves the recommended setpoints, while routine adjustments can be automated within predefined guardrails.

The outcome is a more proactive process: less rework, lower energy use per tonne, and more consistent quality. The same approach can be applied to ovens, dryers, kilns, and mills.

Figure 5. A forecast of product quality helps the operator evaluate freezer setpoints before making an adjustment.

Use Case 2 | Anomaly detection: from a flag to the right action

A store operations team monitors sales for thousands of products across hundreds of stores. Fixed thresholds often flag predictable weekend peaks while missing quieter changes, such as a product selling less than expected. As alerts accumulate, it becomes harder for the team to know where to focus.

AI_DETECT_ANOMALIES gives each sales series an expected range based on its recent history. Each new reading is compared with that range at a confidence level the team chooses, without training a separate model for every product and store.

When sales fall outside the expected range, the signal can be combined with inventory and store data to help identify a likely cause and recommend a next step—for example, checking the shelf or replenishing stock. The same approach can be applied to machine sensors, API telemetry, meter readings, and payment volumes.

Figure 6. Store sales are compared with an expected range. In the view shown, recurring peaks remain within the range and no anomaly is flagged.

Use Case 3 | Supply chain planning: every SKU, every store, every hour

A category planner and a replenishment team need to keep products available across every store without carrying excess inventory. But forecasts may be refreshed only once a week, often focusing on top-selling products, while the long tail is managed with simpler rules. When sales patterns change between planning cycles, one store can run out while another has too much stock.

With AI_FORECAST, a pretrained model can forecast demand across products and stores. In this example, it produces a 28-day forecast with a P10–P90 range, refreshed as new sales data arrives. The planning application combines the forecast with inventory, lead time, and the planner’s chosen service level to calculate a reorder point.

When stock is projected to fall below that point, an agent can draft a purchase order for review. The same approach can support planning for spare parts, staffing, ATM cash, and energy demand.

Figure 7. A store-level demand forecast informs a reorder point and a proposed purchase order for oat milk.

Use Case 4 | Fraud and security: every card has its own normal

Fraud teams already rely on sophisticated rules and models to evaluate transactions. One continuing challenge is that a threshold applied across many cardholders may not reflect how each person normally spends.

A time-series signal can add that individual context. In this example, each payment is compared with an expected spending range based on the card’s recent history. A transaction outside that range is passed to the bank’s existing fraud systems as an additional input, alongside other signals and business rules.

The bank can then decide whether to approve the payment, request additional authentication, or investigate further. The decision and the signals behind it can be retained for review.

Figure 8.A payment outside the card’s expected spending range prompts a step-up authentication in an illustrative fraud workflow.

Use Case 5 | Trading: pace the order with the tape

An execution desk needs to divide a large order into smaller trades while managing its effect on the market. Historical volume curves offer a starting point, but today’s trading activity may look very different from the average.

On each one-minute bar, PatchTST-FM forecasts trading volume for the next 30 minutes, with a P10–P90 range. The execution algorithm uses that forecast to pace the order within the participation limit set by the desk.

If a news event changes market activity, the algorithm can pause and replan. If trading is quieter than expected, it can reduce the size of each slice and signal that the order may take longer to complete. Each forecast and the resulting execution decisions can be retained in the audit trail.

Figure 9. Volume forecast informs the proposed execution schedule for a 100,000-share order.

Use Case 6 | Semantic search: find every signal that looks like this

A reliability engineer investigating an unusual sensor pattern may want to know whether similar behavior appeared elsewhere in the plant.

TSPulse can produce representations of time-series windows that support similarity search. In a separately built application, those representations could be indexed and used to retrieve historical patterns across equipment. An engineer could search for shapes such as a spike and recovery, a gradual rise, or a step change, then inspect the associated maintenance records and operating conditions.

This application requires an embedding pipeline, an index, and access to the relevant context. Similarity can help narrow an investigation; it does not establish a root cause by itself.

Figure 10. Time-series embeddings can support a search for similar patterns across equipment and other signals.

Industry Specific Applications

The same models and building blocks can support different workflows across industries:

  • Industrial AI: from sensor to setpoint. The plant manager wants every batch in spec and no line stopped by a surprise. SCADA, QA lab and energy meter streams are forecast as they arrive. Production optimization moves the setpoints when quality starts to drift, anomaly detection flags the reading no rule was written for, and semantic search finds every pump that showed the same pattern before a failure. Setpoints, work orders and alerts reach the floor inside the cycle, not at the next shift report.

Figure 11. The plant twin, from sensor to setpoint. A new cream lot pulls overrun off target. The forecast reads the line, the agent proposes a new draw temperature and air flow, the operator approves, and the tubs are back in spec. Simulated data.

  • Retail: a store and its supply chain. The store manager wants a full shelf on Saturday without overstock on Monday. Sales, weather and promotion streams are forecast for every product in every store. Supply chain planning sets the order, anomaly detection catches the empty shelf or the missed delivery, and fraud and security holds the suspicious card. Orders, store tasks and holds go out before the shelf runs empty.

Figure 12. The store twin, a store and its supply chain. A promo is coming for oat milk. The forecast prices in the promo and sets the reorder point, the agent raises a purchase order, the planner approves, and the shelf is full on promo day. Simulated data.

  • Banking: payments and the trading desk. The fraud lead wants to stop card testing without blocking good customers, and the trader wants a large order done without moving the price. Every card and every symbol is scored against its own expected pattern, event by event. Fraud and security holds the odd swipe before authorization, anomaly detection spots the unusual flow, and trading paces each order with the forecast volume.

  • Airlines: hub operations, fleet and network. Operations control wants to see a disruption coming while there is still time to act. Engine, gate and network streams are forecast and checked in real time. Anomaly detection catches the engine reading that drifts, production optimization rebalances gates and crews, and supply chain planning puts the spare part where the aircraft will be.

In every industry, the Streamhouse does the same work: Flink runs the Granite models to forecast, detect and optimize, Streaming Agents act on the live context, and people approve the exceptions.

Explore the models on Confluent to see how time-series intelligence can support real-time decisions.

Learn more

Real-time forecasting, anomaly detection, and optimization, powered by IBM time-series models with more than 50 million downloads. Now available natively on Confluent, in the cloud and on premises, running on CPUs.
Every business generates a continuous record of change: a machine reading, a payment, a sale, an order, or a change in inventory. These observations form time series, and they carry signals that can help teams anticipate what happens next.
The challenge is turning those signals into decisions while they still matter. A forecast delivered after a production run, a stockout, or a payment authorization may be accurate, but too late to influence the outcome.
IBM and Confluent are bringing time-series foundation models closer to the data as it flows. With Apache Flink, teams can apply forecasting , anomaly detection and semantic intelligence to streaming data using SQL, making model outputs available to the applications and people responsible for the next action. 
Foundation models have changed how organizations work with text, images, and documents. Time-series foundation models extend a similar idea to numerical data by learning general patterns from diverse historical data and then applying that knowledge to new series and tasks. The models can provide a starting point without requiring teams to train a separate model for every series. Depending on the task and deployment, teams can also fine-tune a model or combine its outputs with other data and business logic. 

Figure 1. More than 50 million downloads, and the family of four models behind them
Now the time series foundation models run natively inside Confluent as built-in functions in the cloud and on premises. In Confluent Cloud they are fully managed, with nothing to deploy (documentation). On premises, the models can run within your own infrastructure using Confluent Platform for Apache Flink.(documentation). The models run on CPUs, without requiring GPUs.
The models can support a range of mission-critical use cases, from helping keep production lines in spec and detecting unusual store activity to improving product-level planning. They can also provide signals to assess card payments and forecast trading volume to help place large orders. These building blocks can be applied across manufacturing, retail, banking, and airlines, bringing insights closer to where decisions are made.
See how time series and real-time context come together to create value:





Streamhouse: real-time data and intelligence for agentic era


Businesses operate continuously. Orders are updated, payments arrive, shipments are delayed, and inventory changes throughout the day. Yet the information behind these events often sits across systems that update at different times or rely on periodic batch processes. When applications and AI agents act on outdated or inconsistent information, they risk making decisions that no longer reflect what is happening.
A Streamhouse addresses this by continuously capturing, processing, governing, and serving current business context. Confluent’s Data Streaming Platform brings together five capabilities—connect, stream, process, govern, and query—to make that context available to applications, analytics, and agents. Apache Flink transforms and enriches data as it flows, while Lightning Tables provide low-latency access to the current state. 

Figure 2. The Streamhouse on Confluent: from existing data sources to current business context that agents, applications, analytics and lakehouses use anywhere.
Time-series models add predictive power to this architecture. Flink can prepare the data, invoke forecasting and anomaly detection, and make the results available alongside the events that produced them. Other models—including large language models, statistical models, and specialized machine learning systems—can contribute where appropriate.

Figure 3. The intelligence layer of the Streamhouse: time series models, large language models, and ML and statistical models, with orchestration across them.
This approach can help teams in four ways:
-Scale model development. A pretrained model can provide a common starting point across many time series, reducing the need to develop and maintain a separate model for each one.
-Refresh predictions as data changes. Forecasts can incorporate recent observations as part of a streaming workflow, subject to the model’s requirements and the pipeline’s configuration.
-Put signals closer to decisions. Forecasts and anomalies can be routed to operational applications sooner, where teams can combine them with business context, rules, and human judgment.
-Run compact models on CPUs. The models are small enough to run on standard CPUs alongside the streaming pipeline, in the cloud or on premises, which can reduce the need for dedicated GPU infrastructure and simplify deployment.

Figure 4. Stream native time-series intelligence on Confluent




Mission-critical use cases across real-enterprises


The following scenarios illustrate how organizations could combine time-series models, streaming data, and application logic.




Use Case 1 | Production optimization: every tub in spec


An ice cream line’s quality depends on overrun—the amount of air whipped into the mix. Today, the process engineer and operator rely on QA lab measurements taken after the tubs are filled. If a new cream lot or a warm, humid day changes the process, hours of production may already need rework by the time the team sees the result.
To get ahead of the problem, a pretrained TTM model reads SCADA telemetry and QA measurements every 10 minutes. It forecasts the share of tubs expected to be in spec four hours ahead, along with a likely range.
When the forecast falls below the plant’s target, an optimization process evaluates combinations of freezer draw temperature and airflow. Because the model takes these control variables as inputs, it can score each option before anything changes on the line. The operator approves the recommended setpoints, while routine adjustments can be automated within predefined guardrails.
The outcome is a more proactive process: less rework, lower energy use per tonne, and more consistent quality. The same approach can be applied to ovens, dryers, kilns, and mills.

Figure 5. A forecast of product quality helps the operator evaluate freezer setpoints before making an adjustment.




Use Case 2 | Anomaly detection: from a flag to the right action


A store operations team monitors sales for thousands of products across hundreds of stores. Fixed thresholds often flag predictable weekend peaks while missing quieter changes, such as a product selling less than expected. As alerts accumulate, it becomes harder for the team to know where to focus.
AI_DETECT_ANOMALIES gives each sales series an expected range based on its recent history. Each new reading is compared with that range at a confidence level the team chooses, without training a separate model for every product and store.
When sales fall outside the expected range, the signal can be combined with inventory and store data to help identify a likely cause and recommend a next step—for example, checking the shelf or replenishing stock. The same approach can be applied to machine sensors, API telemetry, meter readings, and payment volumes.

Figure 6. Store sales are compared with an expected range. In the view shown, recurring peaks remain within the range and no anomaly is flagged.




Use Case 3 | Supply chain planning: every SKU, every store, every hour


A category planner and a replenishment team need to keep products available across every store without carrying excess inventory. But forecasts may be refreshed only once a week, often focusing on top-selling products, while the long tail is managed with simpler rules. When sales patterns change between planning cycles, one store can run out while another has too much stock.
With AI_FORECAST, a pretrained model can forecast demand across products and stores. In this example, it produces a 28-day forecast with a P10–P90 range, refreshed as new sales data arrives. The planning application combines the forecast with inventory, lead time, and the planner’s chosen service level to calculate a reorder point.
When stock is projected to fall below that point, an agent can draft a purchase order for review. The same approach can support planning for spare parts, staffing, ATM cash, and energy demand.

Figure 7. A store-level demand forecast informs a reorder point and a proposed purchase order for oat milk.




Use Case 4 | Fraud and security: every card has its own normal


Fraud teams already rely on sophisticated rules and models to evaluate transactions. One continuing challenge is that a threshold applied across many cardholders may not reflect how each person normally spends.
A time-series signal can add that individual context. In this example, each payment is compared with an expected spending range based on the card’s recent history. A transaction outside that range is passed to the bank’s existing fraud systems as an additional input, alongside other signals and business rules.
The bank can then decide whether to approve the payment, request additional authentication, or investigate further. The decision and the signals behind it can be retained for review.

Figure 8.A payment outside the card’s expected spending range prompts a step-up authentication in an illustrative fraud workflow.




Use Case 5 | Trading: pace the order with the tape


An execution desk needs to divide a large order into smaller trades while managing its effect on the market. Historical volume curves offer a starting point, but today’s trading activity may look very different from the average.
On each one-minute bar, PatchTST-FM forecasts trading volume for the next 30 minutes, with a P10–P90 range. The execution algorithm uses that forecast to pace the order within the participation limit set by the desk.
If a news event changes market activity, the algorithm can pause and replan. If trading is quieter than expected, it can reduce the size of each slice and signal that the order may take longer to complete. Each forecast and the resulting execution decisions can be retained in the audit trail.

Figure 9. Volume forecast informs the proposed execution schedule for a 100,000-share order.




Use Case 6 | Semantic search: find every signal that looks like this


A reliability engineer investigating an unusual sensor pattern may want to know whether similar behavior appeared elsewhere in the plant.
TSPulse can produce representations of time-series windows that support similarity search. In a separately built application, those representations could be indexed and used to retrieve historical patterns across equipment. An engineer could search for shapes such as a spike and recovery, a gradual rise, or a step change, then inspect the associated maintenance records and operating conditions.
This application requires an embedding pipeline, an index, and access to the relevant context. Similarity can help narrow an investigation; it does not establish a root cause by itself.

Figure 10. Time-series embeddings can support a search for similar patterns across equipment and other signals.




Industry Specific Applications


The same models and building blocks can support different workflows across industries:
Industrial AI: from sensor to setpoint. The plant manager wants every batch in spec and no line stopped by a surprise. SCADA, QA lab and energy meter streams are forecast as they arrive. Production optimization moves the setpoints when quality starts to drift, anomaly detection flags the reading no rule was written for, and semantic search finds every pump that showed the same pattern before a failure. Setpoints, work orders and alerts reach the floor inside the cycle, not at the next shift report.

Figure 11. The plant twin, from sensor to setpoint. A new cream lot pulls overrun off target. The forecast reads the line, the agent proposes a new draw temperature and air flow, the operator approves, and the tubs are back in spec. Simulated data.
Retail: a store and its supply chain. The store manager wants a full shelf on Saturday without overstock on Monday. Sales, weather and promotion streams are forecast for every product in every store. Supply chain planning sets the order, anomaly detection catches the empty shelf or the missed delivery, and fraud and security holds the suspicious card. Orders, store tasks and holds go out before the shelf runs empty.

Figure 12. The store twin, a store and its supply chain. A promo is coming for oat milk. The forecast prices in the promo and sets the reorder point, the agent raises a purchase order, the planner approves, and the shelf is full on promo day. Simulated data.
Banking: payments and the trading desk. The fraud lead wants to stop card testing without blocking good customers, and the trader wants a large order done without moving the price. Every card and every symbol is scored against its own expected pattern, event by event. Fraud and security holds the odd swipe before authorization, anomaly detection spots the unusual flow, and trading paces each order with the forecast volume.
Airlines: hub operations, fleet and network. Operations control wants to see a disruption coming while there is still time to act. Engine, gate and network streams are forecast and checked in real time. Anomaly detection catches the engine reading that drifts, production optimization rebalances gates and crews, and supply chain planning puts the spare part where the aircraft will be.
In every industry, the Streamhouse does the same work: Flink runs the Granite models to forecast, detect and optimize, Streaming Agents act on the live context, and people approve the exceptions.
Explore the models on Confluent to see how time-series intelligence can support real-time decisions.





Learn more

items.title: 180B Parameters, 32GB of RAM: Pushing MoE Inference to the Limit with Transformers
items.content:
Update on GitHub

Streaming MoE experts directly from SSD gets within 6% of Strata on token generation.

I've been trying to rely less on online models and run bigger ones locally. At home I have a PC with two RTX 4090s (let's call it Orthrus - the two-headed hound of Greek mythology), and for work I have a MacBook M5 with 32G of unified memory.

Orthrus runs on Windows 11, because my kids play games all the time. I had a dual boot with Ubuntu, but their games ended up taking most of the two terabytes of disk.

I am also a huge fan of RMD (rooms moving development): one hour in the kitchen sipping my coffee, two hours at my office desk, then the sofa. A fixed desktop tower is not for me.

My first experiment was to run Qwen 3.8 27B with llama.app on Orthrus and use it from my laptop through pi. That model does the coding tasks, an online model like Opus does the orchestration, and the second RTX runs a FIM model for auto-completion in Neovim.

When I talked about this on social networks, I got very strong feedback: use Strata with Qwen3.8-Flash-Next.

What is Strata?

Strata is an inference engine for MoE models like Qwen. Only the hot experts stay in VRAM, the rest goes to RAM, or even to disk. Experts are 90%+ of a MoE model's weights, so a 180B model like this one can run on a GPU with much less memory. Like my RTX 4090!

It works on a laptop too, and I stumbled on this blog post doing exactly that: Qwen3.8-Flash-Next on a 32 GB Mac M4, faster than llama.cpp, at 13.5 tok/s.

That's too slow for how I use coding agents, but it's an interesting itch to scratch. A whole range of MoE models don't fit in a MacBook's unified memory and could run at a decent speed.

How do other engines offload?

Before committing to Strata, I looked at what llama.cpp, vLLM and Transformers do when a MoE model doesn't fit. Three questions matter: where do the experts live, where does the expert matmul run, and what moves on each token?

llama.cpp maps the GGUF file with mmap and can keep the experts on the CPU (--cpu-moe, --n-cpu-moe N, -ot "exps=CPU", or --fit on to pick for you). Those experts are also computed on the CPU, so only the activations cross PCIe, never the weights. Great when the experts fit in RAM. When they don't, the page cache thrashes. A GPU expert cache (--moe-cache-mib) just landed, but it fragments the graph (2 splits per token become 50) and loses ~10% even when everything fits.

vLLM's --cpu-offload-gb N puts N GB of weights in pinned RAM, and kernels read them in place over PCIe. For a MoE layer, that's only the routed experts, but nothing is cached: a hot expert crosses PCIe again on every token, and there's no disk tier. By default the offloaded weights include dense layers, read on every token; --cpu-offload-params experts keeps it to the experts. That fits vLLM's big batches, which touch almost every expert anyway, less so one user on one GPU.

Transformers offloads through Accelerate (device_map="auto", offload_folder), one module at a time: hooks copy its weights to the GPU before forward. For a MoE, that module is a layer's whole expert bank, so every token copies every expert of every offloaded layer to use 8 or 10 of them. No cache, no notion of routing. And on a Mac, CPU and GPU share the same memory, so "offload to CPU" frees nothing.

I ran all of them on Qwen3.6-35B-A3B on one A10G (24 GB), with plenty of RAM, and Harry Mellor reran vLLM with better flags:

Engine Decode (tok/s)
Strata, Q8_0 82 - 88
llama.cpp, Q8_0, --fit on 63 - 64
llama.cpp, BF16, --fit on 35 - 36
vLLM, FP8, --cpu-offload-gb 16 --cpu-offload-params experts 20.1
vLLM, FP8, same flags, --enforce-eager 14.7
vLLM, FP8, --cpu-offload-gb 16 9.7
vLLM, BF16, --cpu-offload-gb 50 --cpu-offload-params experts 7.3
vLLM, BF16, --cpu-offload-gb 50 3.3
Transformers + Accelerate 0.16

Offloading only the experts doubles vLLM's speed, and FP8 helps on top (half the bytes per expert, more of the model on the GPU). vLLM's other offload backend, which copies groups of layers ahead of time, ran under 1 tok/s.

If the experts fit in RAM, llama.cpp is hard to beat. If they don't, you have to stream only what the router picks, through a bounded cache, fast enough that the SSD is the bottleneck and not Python, ideally reusing the model's fast expert kernels. That's Qwen3.8-Flash-Next on a 32 GB Mac, and Transformers couldn't do it out of the box.

Making Qwen3.8-Flash-Next work on my 32 GB Mac with Transformers

Strata was already too slow for me on the laptop, and Transformers was not going to beat it anytime soon. But the Accelerate path was so far off that I wanted to try fixing offloading in Transformers itself, with the big model on my laptop as the target, knowing it would probably stay too slow for how I work.

All of the code was built with AI: the Transformers PR, the model-specific package and the Metal kernels. My part was choosing what to try, reading the profiles, and deciding what to keep. Everything is in a Space: tarekziade/moe-expert-streaming.

Start small

I started with OLMoE-1B-7B, which fits in memory, so I could compare every token with vanilla Transformers.

First version: experts on disk, an LRU cache on the device, and a Python loop running one expert at a time. With every expert already cached, it did 10.1 tok/s. Vanilla did ~32. The I/O was fine, my loop was not: vanilla uses grouped_mm, which runs all the experts of a layer in one kernel.

The fix, and the key idea of this project, was to turn the cache into a slot pool: one preallocated device tensor shared by all layers, plus a per-layer table from expert id to slot. Remap the router's expert ids to slots and the pool looks like a regular expert bank, so grouped_mm runs on it as is. No custom expert matmul needed. That got it to 34.6 tok/s, against 38.1 for vanilla.

experts_offload

I then turned the standalone loader into an option of from_pretrained, in huggingface/transformers#50717. To try it, install Transformers from that PR:

pip install "git+https://github.com/huggingface/transformers.git@refs/pull/50717/head"

Then, moving from OLMoE to the real target, Qwen3.8-Flash-Next:

path = snapshot_download("tarekziade/Qwen3.8-Flash-Next-expert-streaming")

model = AutoModelForCausalLM.from_pretrained(
    f"{path}/dense",
    dtype=torch.bfloat16,
    device_map={"": "mps", "experts.*": "disk"},
    quantization_config=MetalConfig(bits=8),
    experts_offload={
        "cache_bytes": 12 << 30,
        "quantized_experts": f"{path}/experts-q3",
    },
)

That repo holds the output of the project's conversion script: the dense weights, the experts quantized to 3 bits, and the n-gram table.

Experts mapped to "disk" go through the streaming path instead of Accelerate's offload: the loader skips their tensors and MoE layers switch to an offloaded implementation. Misses are read by 8 I/O threads, one contiguous read per expert. The next two layers' routers run early on the current hidden states to guess which experts to prefetch. Experts can be quantized offline so reads are smaller. It works for MoE models with the standard experts layout.

The API is still being discussed with the Transformers maintainers. The device_map form came out of that, and quantized experts will probably go through the per-layer quantization plan of #50245 rather than their own option.

Running 121 GB of experts on a 32 GB Mac

Qwen3.8-Flash-Next has 48 layers of 512 experts (10 active), 121 GB in FP8. Streaming them isn't enough: there's also a 51 GB n-gram embedding table that needs its own disk path. So:

  • experts quantized to 3 bits: 49 GB on disk, 12 GiB cached on the device
  • dense layers in 8 bits (~5.4 GB, +0.2% perplexity vs BF16)
  • the n-gram table stays on disk, rows read when needed

The conversion takes ~5 hours. After loading, it uses ~18 GiB, and a 6K prompt peaks at 25.4 GiB. That's about the limit: I have to close the browser, or macOS starts swapping.

The model-specific bits (the n-gram table, Metal kernels) live in a small package, moe-expert-streaming, on top of the PR. The first version ran at about 10 tok/s.

Then I installed Strata on the same M5, with the same prompts:

Transformers Strata Gap
Decode, 200 tokens 10.0 tok/s 14.8 1.5x
Prefill, 4K prompt 68 tok/s 220 3.2x
Decode after a 6K document 7.3 tok/s 13.7 1.9x

Strata 0.1.60 used IQ3_XXS experts. Both ran greedy, with thinking, MTP and speculative drafts off, and 1,024-token prefill chunks. The full setup and raw results are on the Space's details page.

I also tried vllm-metal, vLLM on Apple GPUs through MLX, which recently got expert offloading. It streams the routed experts from an MLX checkpoint through a bounded cache, like this project. But it can't run Qwen3.8-Flash-Next on 32 GB, for the n-gram reason above: only the experts are streamed, and the n-gram tables stay in memory. That's 32 GB in the MLX checkpoints on the Hub, before the ~5 GB of dense layers and any expert cache.

Closing the gap

Most of the time wasn't spent on experts. Here's what helped:

  • Committing GPU work early. PyTorch on MPS holds small kernels until the next sync, so the GPU idled while Python worked. Forcing a commit after each block gave +10%. This should really be fixed in PyTorch.
  • Metal kernels for the parts without a fast path on macOS: Gated DeltaNet and the hyper-connections.
  • Strata's own weights. I switched to Strata's GGUF weights, reducing dense weight traffic from 5.4 GB to 3.9 GB per token and individual expert size from 2.15 MB to 1.75 MB, with a separate cache pool for each expert size.
  • Prefill, we went from 68 to ~228 tok/s using bigger chunks, and reading the next layer's experts while the current layer is being computed.
  • Long documents: attention over the indexer's selected blocks only, and a KV cache that grows in place instead of being copied at every token.
  • Misses: Strata doesn't hide them, it waits like I do, and no cache policy beat LRU by much. What helped was reading just one guessed expert per layer, while the SSD would otherwise be idle.

Here's one MoE layer for one token, as it runs now:

These are the final results after these optimizations on the same M5 with the same prompts:

Transformers Strata Gap
Decode, 200 tokens 13.9 tok/s 14.8 1.06x
Prefill, 4K prompt 228 tok/s 220 1.0x
Decode after a 6K document 12.4 tok/s 13.7 1.1x

That's about 6% behind Strata on short decode, with slightly faster prefill, all through Transformers.

Most of what's left is host round trips, ~10 ms per token. Waking up after a sync is only ~1 ms of that. The rest is the GPU running dry while Python queues the next layer. Strata queues the whole token's work up front, and the GPU waits on a Metal shared event at each layer while the host reads experts. PyTorch doesn't expose that. I tried to fake it with a kernel spinning on a flag the CPU writes, and the GPU took anywhere from a second to never to see the write. The real fix would be a native op on PyTorch's MPS stream, with a risk of hangs, so I haven't built it.

Conclusion

It runs at ~14 tok/s, close to Strata, and it's still too slow for how I use coding agents. Orthrus keeps doing the real work.

Transformers didn't beat Strata, and closing the last ~6% would take deeper changes in the stack, starting with control over that per-layer sync, which PyTorch doesn't give you today. The interesting part is how it got that close: streaming only the routed experts, a bounded cache that grouped_mm runs on as is, and a few targeted Metal kernels. There's no C++ extension in the project: just Python, Metal kernels compiled at runtime with torch.mps.compile_shader, and prebuilt kernels from the Hub. All the Metal kernels written for this experiment are now published on the Hub, and the project loads them from there.

Beating Strata was never the only goal, though. Building this was a great way to learn how MoEs and LLMs work from a systems perspective: how sparse the routing really is, how much an expert cache buys you, where memory bandwidth goes per token, and how much time the host and the GPU spend waiting on each other. Transformers makes all of that easy to poke at, one module at a time.

The generic expert streaming implementation is in huggingface/transformers#50717, and the benchmarks are in the Space. Feedback on the approach and the API is welcome.

Thanks to Pedro, Lysandre and Arthur for their excellent feedback, and to Harry for helping test vLLM.

Finally, thanks to Niko Veit for Strata. Strata set the bar for what's possible with expert streaming on consumer hardware, and having those numbers to chase is what pushed this work as far as it went.

don't, the page cache thrashes. A GPU expert cache (--moe-cache-mib) just
landed, but it fragments the graph (2 splits per token become 50) and loses
~10% even when everything fits.
vLLM's --cpu-offload-gb N puts N GB of weights in pinned RAM, and kernels
read them in place over PCIe. For a MoE layer, that's only the routed experts,
but nothing is cached: a hot expert crosses PCIe again on every token, and
there's no disk tier. By default the offloaded weights include dense layers,
read on every token; --cpu-offload-params experts keeps it to the experts. That fits vLLM's big
batches, which touch almost every expert anyway, less so one user on one GPU.
Transformers offloads through Accelerate (device_map="auto",
offload_folder), one module at a time: hooks copy its weights to the GPU
before forward. For a MoE, that module is a layer's whole expert bank, so
every token copies every expert of every offloaded layer to use 8 or 10 of them.
No cache, no notion of routing. And on a Mac, CPU and GPU share the same memory,
so "offload to CPU" frees nothing.
I ran all of them on Qwen3.6-35B-A3B on one A10G (24 GB), with plenty of RAM,
and Harry Mellor reran vLLM with better flags:

Engine
Decode (tok/s)



Strata, Q8_0
82 - 88


llama.cpp, Q8_0, --fit on
63 - 64


llama.cpp, BF16, --fit on
35 - 36


vLLM, FP8, --cpu-offload-gb 16 --cpu-offload-params experts
20.1


vLLM, FP8, same flags, --enforce-eager
14.7


vLLM, FP8, --cpu-offload-gb 16
9.7


vLLM, BF16, --cpu-offload-gb 50 --cpu-offload-params experts
7.3


vLLM, BF16, --cpu-offload-gb 50
3.3


Transformers + Accelerate
0.16




Offloading only the experts doubles vLLM's speed, and FP8 helps on top (half
the bytes per expert, more of the model on the GPU). vLLM's other offload
backend, which copies groups of layers ahead of time, ran under 1 tok/s.
If the experts fit in RAM, llama.cpp is hard to beat. If they don't, you have to
stream only what the router picks, through a bounded cache, fast enough that the
SSD is the bottleneck and not Python, ideally reusing the model's fast expert
kernels. That's Qwen3.8-Flash-Next on a 32 GB Mac, and Transformers couldn't do
it out of the box.




Making Qwen3.8-Flash-Next work on my 32 GB Mac with Transformers


Strata was already too slow for me on the laptop, and Transformers was not going
to beat it anytime soon. But the Accelerate path was so far off that I wanted to
try fixing offloading in Transformers itself, with the big model on my laptop as
the target, knowing it would probably stay too slow for how I work.
All of the code was built with AI: the Transformers PR, the model-specific
package and the Metal kernels. My part was choosing what to try, reading the
profiles, and deciding what to keep. Everything is in a Space:
tarekziade/moe-expert-streaming.




Start small


I started with OLMoE-1B-7B, which fits in memory, so I could compare every token
with vanilla Transformers.
First version: experts on disk, an LRU cache on the device, and a Python loop
running one expert at a time. With every expert already cached, it did 10.1
tok/s. Vanilla did ~32. The I/O was fine, my loop was not: vanilla uses
grouped_mm, which runs all the experts of a layer in one kernel.
The fix, and the key idea of this project, was to turn the cache into a slot
pool: one preallocated device tensor shared by all layers, plus a per-layer
table from expert id to slot. Remap the router's expert ids to slots and the
pool looks like a regular expert bank, so grouped_mm runs on it as is. No
custom expert matmul needed. That got it to 34.6 tok/s, against 38.1 for
vanilla.




experts_offload


I then turned the standalone loader into an option of from_pretrained, in
huggingface/transformers#50717.
To try it, install Transformers from that PR:
pip install "git+https://github.com/huggingface/transformers.git@refs/pull/50717/head"

Then, moving from OLMoE to the real target, Qwen3.8-Flash-Next:
path = snapshot_download("tarekziade/Qwen3.8-Flash-Next-expert-streaming")

model = AutoModelForCausalLM.from_pretrained(
    f"{path}/dense",
    dtype=torch.bfloat16,
    device_map={"": "mps", "experts.*": "disk"},
    quantization_config=MetalConfig(bits=8),
    experts_offload={
        "cache_bytes": 12 << 30,
        "quantized_experts": f"{path}/experts-q3",
    },
)

That repo
holds the output of the project's
conversion script:
the dense weights, the experts quantized to 3 bits, and the n-gram table.
Experts mapped to "disk" go through the streaming path instead of Accelerate's
offload: the loader skips their tensors and MoE layers switch to an offloaded
implementation. Misses are read by 8 I/O threads, one contiguous read per
expert. The next two layers' routers run early on the current hidden states to
guess which experts to prefetch. Experts can be quantized offline so reads are
smaller. It works for MoE models with the standard experts layout.
The API is still being discussed with the Transformers maintainers. The
device_map form came out of that, and quantized experts will probably go
through the per-layer quantization plan of
#50245 rather than
their own option.




Running 121 GB of experts on a 32 GB Mac


Qwen3.8-Flash-Next has 48 layers of 512 experts (10 active), 121 GB in FP8.
Streaming them isn't enough: there's also a 51 GB n-gram embedding
table that needs its own disk path. So:
experts quantized to 3 bits: 49 GB on disk, 12 GiB cached on the device
dense layers in 8 bits (~5.4 GB, +0.2% perplexity vs BF16)
the n-gram table stays on disk, rows read when needed
The conversion takes ~5 hours. After loading, it uses ~18 GiB, and a 6K prompt
peaks at 25.4 GiB. That's about the limit: I have to close the browser, or macOS
starts swapping.
The model-specific bits (the n-gram table, Metal kernels) live in a small
package, moe-expert-streaming,
on top of the PR. The first version ran at about 10 tok/s.
Then I installed Strata on the same M5, with the same prompts:


Transformers
Strata
Gap



Decode, 200 tokens
10.0 tok/s
14.8
1.5x


Prefill, 4K prompt
68 tok/s
220
3.2x


Decode after a 6K document
7.3 tok/s
13.7
1.9x




Strata 0.1.60 used IQ3_XXS experts. Both ran greedy, with thinking, MTP and
speculative drafts off, and 1,024-token prefill chunks. The full setup and raw
results are on the Space's
details page.
I also tried vllm-metal, vLLM on
Apple GPUs through MLX, which recently got expert offloading. It streams the
routed experts from an MLX checkpoint through a bounded cache, like this
project. But it can't run Qwen3.8-Flash-Next on 32 GB, for the n-gram reason
above: only the experts are streamed, and the n-gram tables stay in memory.
That's 32 GB in the MLX checkpoints on the Hub, before the ~5 GB of dense layers and any expert cache.




Closing the gap


Most of the time wasn't spent on experts. Here's what helped:
Committing GPU work early. PyTorch on MPS holds small kernels until the
next sync, so the GPU idled while Python worked. Forcing a commit after each
block gave +10%. This should really be fixed in PyTorch.
Metal kernels for the parts without a fast path on macOS: Gated DeltaNet
and the hyper-connections.
Strata's own weights. I switched to Strata's GGUF weights, reducing dense
weight traffic from 5.4 GB to 3.9 GB per token and individual expert size from
2.15 MB to 1.75 MB, with a separate cache pool for each expert size.
Prefill, we went from 68 to ~228 tok/s using bigger chunks, and reading the next layer's
experts while the current layer is being computed.
Long documents: attention over the indexer's selected blocks only, and a
KV cache that grows in place instead of being copied at every token.
Misses: Strata doesn't hide them, it waits like I do, and no cache policy
beat LRU by much. What helped was reading just one guessed expert per layer,
while the SSD would otherwise be idle.
Here's one MoE layer for one token, as it runs now:

These are the final results after these optimizations on the same M5 with the same prompts:


Transformers
Strata
Gap



Decode, 200 tokens
13.9 tok/s
14.8
1.06x


Prefill, 4K prompt
228 tok/s
220
1.0x


Decode after a 6K document
12.4 tok/s
13.7
1.1x




That's about 6% behind Strata on short decode, with slightly faster prefill,
all through Transformers.
Most of what's left is host round trips, ~10 ms per token. Waking up after a
sync is only ~1 ms of that. The rest is the GPU running dry while Python queues
the next layer. Strata queues the whole token's work up front, and the GPU waits
on a Metal shared event at each layer while the host reads experts. PyTorch
doesn't expose that. I tried to fake it with a kernel spinning on a flag the CPU
writes, and the GPU took anywhere from a second to never to see the write. The
real fix would be a native op on PyTorch's MPS stream, with a risk of hangs, so
I haven't built it.




Conclusion


It runs at ~14 tok/s, close to Strata, and it's still too slow for how I use
coding agents. Orthrus keeps doing the real work.
Transformers didn't beat Strata, and closing the last ~6% would take deeper
changes in the stack, starting with control over that per-layer sync, which
PyTorch doesn't give you today. The interesting part is how it got that
close: streaming only the routed experts, a bounded cache that grouped_mm runs
on as is, and a few targeted Metal kernels. There's no C++ extension in the
project: just Python, Metal kernels compiled at runtime with
torch.mps.compile_shader, and prebuilt kernels from the Hub.
All the Metal kernels written for this experiment are now
published on the Hub,
and the project loads them from there.
Beating Strata was never the only goal, though. Building this was a great way
to learn how MoEs and LLMs work from a systems perspective: how sparse the
routing really is, how much an expert cache buys you, where memory bandwidth
goes per token, and how much time the host and the GPU spend waiting on each
other. Transformers makes all of that easy to poke at, one module at a time.
The generic expert streaming implementation is in
huggingface/transformers#50717,
and the benchmarks are in the Space.
Feedback on the approach and the API is welcome.
Thanks to Pedro, Lysandre and Arthur for their excellent feedback, and to Harry
for helping test vLLM.
Finally, thanks to Niko Veit for Strata.
Strata set the bar for what's possible with expert streaming on consumer
hardware, and having those numbers to chase is what pushed this work as far as
it went.

summaries.zh: 文章主要介绍了如何利用Transformer技术在180B参数、32GB内存的限制下运行MoE模型。作者通过对比Strata、llama.cpp、vLLM和Transformers等推理引擎，发现Strata在MoE模型推理中表现最佳，可将专家直接从SSD流式传输至VRAM，效率接近Strata。此外，作者还探讨了不同引擎在内存不足时的专家卸载策略，并测试了vLLM在FP8量化下的性能提升。实验表明，卸载专家可显著提升速度，FP8量化进一步优化性能。
summaries.en: The article explores running large MoE models like Qwen3.8-27B with limited GPU memory using various inference engines. Strata outperforms other methods, achieving speeds close to Strata on token generation by offloading cold experts to RAM or disk. llama.cpp offloads experts to CPU or GPU, vLLM uses pinned RAM, and Transformers offloads modules sequentially. Benchmark results show Strata and llama.cpp perform best, while vLLM's expert offloading significantly boosts speed. The author tests these engines on a 32GB Mac, finding Strata effective for fitting large models locally.
